sec.title: Background
sec.p: We previously reported a trial using pembrolizumab with a DNA vaccine encoding prostatic acid phosphatase (pTVG-HP) in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). Favorable clinical outcomes were associated with T-cell activation, suggesting immune response to vaccination was critical. In the current trial, we evaluated whether immunization with two vaccines, to broaden the T-cell response to other cancer-associated antigens, would elicit greater anti-tumor efficacy.

sec.title: Materials and methods
sec.p: 60 patients with mCRPC were treated with vaccine on days 1 and 8 of a 3 week cycle, with pembrolizumab given on day 1 of each cycle. Patients in Arm A (n=30) received pTVG-HP as the vaccine, and patients in Arm B (n=30) received pTVG-AR (encoding the ligand-binding domain of the androgen receptor) alternating with pTVG-HP every two cycles. After eight cycles (6 months), patients continued to receive pembrolizumab alone, with the option to receive further booster immunizations at prostate-specific antigen (PSA) progression. The primary objective was 6-month progression-free survival (PFS). Secondary objectives included safety, objective response rate, PSA response rate, overall survival (OS), and immunological evaluations.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Overall median time to progression was 24 weeks (24 weeks Arm A, 24 weeks Arm B, p=0.80). The month 6 PFS rate was 51% in Arm A and 45% in Arm B. Median OS was 2.8 years (2.5 years Arm A, 3.7 years Arm B, p=0.16). 20% of patients in each arm experienced a PSA decline of >50%. 20 patients (n=8 Arm A, n=12 Arm B) had measurable disease, and 6/20 (30%) experienced a partial response. Eight patients received booster immunizations after 6 months, 3 of whom subsequently experienced a PSA decline. Three patients in Arm B experienced creatine kinase elevation with or without increased transaminases, which were not observed in Arm A. T cell immune responses to both antigens were detected in patients treated in Arm B.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Treatment with DNA vaccines and pembrolizumab demonstrated anti-tumor activity in terms of PSA declines and objective responses. The addition of pTVG-AR did not significantly increase measures of clinical efficacy; however, it was associated with a slight increase in toxicity to tissues that also express AR.
Keywords: Prostate Cancer, Combination therapy, Vaccine

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: A DNA vaccine encoding prostatic acid phosphatase (pTVG-HP) was previously explored in combination with PD-1 blockade in the treatment of patients with metastatic, metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC). In that trial, indicators of patient benefit (PSA declines, time on treatment >6 months, overall survival) were associated with markers of T cell activation, suggesting that increasing the magnitude or breadth of T cell response to tumor might further improve the efficacy of this approach.

In the trial reported here, 60 patients with mCRPC were randomized to treatment with one (pTVG-HP) versus two (pTVG-HP and pTVG-AR, encoding the ligand-binding domain of the androgen receptor) DNA vaccines and PD-1 blockade (pembrolizumab). Treatment demonstrated anti-tumor activity in terms of PSA declines and objective responses, but the addition of a second vaccine did not significantly increase measures of clinical efficacy. Rather, this was associated with a slight increase in toxicity.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Future trials using this approach may not require multiple antigens or multiple vaccines in combination with PD-1 blockade. We are currently planning a randomized phase 2 trial using pTVG-HP and PD-1 blockade versus standard of care in patients with advanced mCRPC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) accounts for nearly 36 000 deaths per year in the USA.1 Over the last 20 years, several therapies have been approved by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) based on their ability to prolong overall survival in this mCRPC population, but the median survival benefit of each agent is on the order of 3–4 months, highlighting the need for therapies with greater benefit.2 Among these approved agents are sipuleucel-T, an autologous vaccine that targets the prostate tumor antigen prostatic acid phosphatase (PAP),3 and pembrolizumab, which was approved for a small subset of patients with microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) tumors.4 The approval of these agents demonstrates that immune-based therapies can have a positive role in the treatment of mCRPC. Unfortunately, T-cell checkpoint inhibitors targeting CTLA-4 and/or PD-1/PD-L1, while having substantial activity for some cancer types, have demonstrated little benefit in patients with prostate cancer without high mutational burdens or MSI.5,8 Studies using these agents in combination with other therapies have suggested these may have more activity, and hence combination therapies, including combinations with other immune-targeting agents, are a rational direction to improve their efficacy.9 10

We have previously reported that a DNA vaccine encoding PAP (pTVG-HP, aka MVI-816) could be safely administered to patients with early PSA-recurrent prostate cancer and elicit/augment PAP-specific Th1-biased T cells.11,13 In preclinical studies, we found that vaccination activates CD8+T cells that then express PD-1, and the anti-tumor efficacy of vaccination was improved with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade.14 15 We found that the timing of this blockade was critical, as the efficacy of this combination was primarily due to blockade of PD-L1 on dendritic cells at the time of vaccination from binding PD-1 on vaccine-activated CD8+T cells.16 We tested this approach in a trial of 66 patients with mCRPC using pTVG-HP and pembrolizumab and similarly found that treatment was most effective when vaccination was delivered with concurrent PD-1 blockade.17 18 In that trial, the median progression-free survival (PFS) was 5.6 months, and immune response to the vaccine was associated with PSA declines and increased time on treatment without progression.18 The frequency of vaccination, by delivering vaccines every 2 weeks rather than every 3 weeks, was also found to be associated with greater immune response and longer time to progression.18 These findings suggested that efforts to increase the magnitude or diversity of T cell response to vaccination might lead to superior clinical efficacy.

The current trial was designed to test the hypothesis that increasing the diversity of tumor-specific T-cell activation, by using vaccines targeting more than one cancer-associated target, and when given with concurrent PD-1 blockade, would lead to greater anti-tumor efficacy as measured by time to progression. Patients with mCRPC were randomized to receive one vaccine (pTVG-HP) or two vaccines (pTVG-HP or pTVG-AR, a DNA vaccine encoding the androgen receptor ligand-binding domain (AR LBD), delivered in alternating cycles), and pembrolizumab. The primary endpoint was 6-month PFS. Secondary endpoints included safety, overall objective response rate, overall survival, PSA response rate, and measures of immunological effect.

sec.title: Study agents and regulatory information
sec.p: pTVG-HP (Madison Vaccines, Madison, WI) is a plasmid DNA encoding the full-length human PAP cDNA.19 This vaccine has been previously evaluated in several clinical trials as a monotherapy11 12 20 or in combination with PD-1 blockade.17 18 21 pTVG-AR (Madison Vaccines) is a plasmid DNA encoding the LBD of the androgen receptor,22 23 previously investigated in a phase I trial.24 Pembrolizumab was provided by Merck Sharp & Dohme.

sec.title: Patient population
sec.p: Eligible subjects were those with a histological diagnosis of prostate adenocarcinoma with metastases and evidence of castration resistance. Patients were required to continue androgen deprivation (surgical castration or GnRH analog or antagonist treatment) throughout the study. Patients were required to have progressive disease as defined by consecutive rise in serum PSA pretreatment, and/or increase in disease burden by CT or bone scintigraphy. Prior treatment with second-generation AR pathway inhibitors (ARPI), including abiraterone and/or enzalutamide, or cytotoxic chemotherapy, was allowed, but was to have been discontinued at least 28 days prior to day 1. Patients were required to have an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance score of <2 and adequate bone marrow, liver, and renal function.

sec.title: Study design and procedures
sec.p: This study was designed as an open-label, multi-institution, randomized phase 2 trial to evaluate the immunological and clinical effect of one versus two DNA vaccines, used as T-cell activating therapies, given concurrently with pembrolizumab. Patients in Arm A received 100 µg pTVG-HP administered i.d. on days 1 and 8 of eight 3 week cycles, and 200 mg pembrolizumab was delivered intravenously on day 1 of each cycle. Patients in Arm B received 100 µg DNA vaccine administered i.d., and 200 mg pembrolizumab intravenous, on the same schedule; however, they received pTVG-HP for cycles 3, 4, 7, and 8 and received pTVG-AR for cycles 1, 2, 5, and 6. Each vaccination was delivered in the left deltoid region. The treatment schema is shown in figure 1A. Patients without progression after 8 cycles (6 months) continued to receive pembrolizumab at 3-week intervals for up to two years. If during this time patients experienced a >25% rise in serum PSA, but no radiographic progression, they then underwent four additional cycles of treatment with vaccine (patients on Arm A receiving pTVG-HP on days 1 and 8 of four 3-week cycles, and patients on Arm B receiving pTVG-AR for days 1 and 8 of cycles 1 and 2 and pTVG-HP for days 1 and 8 of cycles 3 and 4). Blood tests were performed every 3 weeks and included complete blood counts (CBC), creatinine, electrolytes, glucose, bilirubin, alanine aminotransferase (ALT), aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alkaline phosphatase, amylase, creatine kinase (CK), cortisol, and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH). All toxicities were graded according to the NCI Common Terminology Criteria Grading System, version 5. For grade 3 events attributed to both pembrolizumab and vaccination, both agents were held until the toxicity resolved to grade 1 or less. Treatment was discontinued if a grade 3 event recurred, or for any grade 4 event. If the adverse event was attributed to pembrolizumab alone, vaccination continued per schedule while holding or discontinuing the pembrolizumab. The accrual goal was 60 patients, testing the hypothesis that treatment with two vaccines would increase the 6-month PFS rate from 20%–25% to 50%–60% with 62%–94% power at the 0.1 significance level.

sec.title: Clinical response evaluation
sec.p: Serum PSA values were collected every 3–6 weeks. CT of abdomen/pelvis and bone scans were obtained within 6 weeks prior to the first day of treatment, and then at 12-week intervals following day 1. Tumor response measurements were made as per Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 recommendations.25 Scans at week 12 were used as the radiographic “baseline” for determining subsequent response or progression in order to permit possible delayed immunological treatment effects and account for possible pseudoprogression. RECIST V.1.1 criteria were used to determine stable disease, partial response, or complete response.25 Patients came off the trial for radiographic progression, clinical progression, or at the discretion of the patient or treating physician; however, discontinuation for PSA rise alone was discouraged.

sec.title: Immunological response evaluation
sec.p: Patients at one center underwent blood draws prior to treatment and at weeks 6, 12, 24, 36, and end of study, for immunological assessments. These patients received a tetanus immunization prior to study treatment as a positive control for immunological testing. Measures of antigen-specific immune response were performed by IFNγ ELISPOT with fresh (not cryopreserved) peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) as previously described, directly ex vivo without in vitro stimulation.20 Antigens used included tetanus toxoid protein (Calbiochem), pools of 15-mer peptides spanning the amino acid sequence of PAP, AR LBD, or PSA and overlapping by 11 amino acids (LifeTein, LLC), or phytohemagglutinin (PHA) as a positive control. A significant immune response to any antigen was defined as an antigen-specific response detectable at least twice post-treatment that was statistically significant (compared with media only control by t-test), at least threefold higher than the pretreatment value, and with a frequency >1:100,000 PBMC, as previously reported.12 17 18 24

Plasma samples were evaluated by Luminex multiplex analysis for 35 cytokine and chemokine analytes, according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Cytokine 35-plex human panel, ThermoFisher). These included EGF, Eotaxin, FGF-basic, G-CSF, GM-CSF, HGF, IFN-alpha, IFN-gamma, IL-1 beta, IL-1 alpha, IL-1RA, IL-2, IL-2R, IL-3, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-7, IL-8, IL-9, IL-10, IL-12 (p40/p70) IL-13, IL-15, IL-17A, IL-17F, IL-22, IP-10, MCP-1, MIG, MIP-1 alpha, MIP-1 beta, RANTES, TNF-alpha, and VEGF.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics were summarized in terms of medians and ranges or frequencies and percentages. Time to radiographic progression was defined from the start of treatment to date of radiographic disease progression or last day of radiographic follow-up. By protocol criteria, radiographic progression was defined using the month 3 scans as the “baseline,” to account for delayed response to immunotherapy. However, patients with evidence of progression at month 3 by scans and rising PSA could be taken off trial for physician discretion. Hence, for the primary analysis, both unconfirmed and confirmed progression events were treated as events for the evaluation of time to radiographic progression. Overall survival was defined from the start of treatment to date of death for any cause or last day of follow-up. Time to radiographic progression and overall survival were analyzed using the Kaplan-Meier method and comparisons between study arms were conducted using the log-rank test. The analysis of efficacy endpoints between study arms was conducted with the intention-to-treat population, which included all randomized participants meeting eligibility criteria. Adverse events with an attribution of at least possibly related to treatment were summarized for each study arm in terms of frequencies, stratified by type and severity (grade). Changes in serum cytokines and chemokines within each arm were evaluated using paired t-tests and comparisons of changes between arms were evaluated using a two-sample t-test. Nominal p values (without multiple testing corrections) were reported due to the exploratory nature of these analyses. Best changes in PSA levels were calculated for each participant as the highest percentage decreases and reported using waterfall plots. The comparisons of overall survival (across both arms) between subjects with PSA declines >50% versus ≤50%, subjects who remained on treatment without progression at 6 months versus discontinued treatment, and immune-related adverse events (irAE) >grade 1 versus no irAEs were performed using a log-rank test. All reported p values are two-sided and p<0.05 was used to define statistical significance. Statistical analyses were conducted using SAS software (SAS Institute), V.9.4.

sec.title: Patient population and adverse events
sec.p: 60 patients with progressive mCRPC were enrolled in this trial between November 2019 and May 2024 at the University of Wisconsin Carbone Cancer Center and the Siteman Cancer Center at Washington University in St. Louis. The data cut-off date for all clinical analyses was 20 June 2025. Patients received vaccination days 1 and 8 of 3 week cycles and pembrolizumab on day 1 of each 3 week cycle. Patients in Arm 1 received one vaccine (pTVG-HP), and patients in Arm 2 received two vaccines (pTVG-HP or pTVG-AR) in an alternating schedule. Patients were treated until month 6 (24 weeks), at which point they continued on pembrolizumab alone at 3-week intervals. Patients with subsequent PSA progression (25% increase), but without radiographic progression, were permitted four additional booster vaccination cycles. The treatment schema is shown in figure 1A, and the allocation of subjects is shown in figure 1B. Demographic information and prior treatments for all patients are shown in table 1. The median age of participants was 71.2 years (range 44–88 years). 80% (48/60) had been treated with a second-generation ARPI in either the castration-sensitive or castration-resistant setting, and 33% (20/60) had received prior taxane chemotherapy (12/60 in the castration-sensitive setting, and 13/60 in the castration-resistant setting). Adverse events are shown in table 2. A single grade 4 event of CK increase was observed in a patient treated in Arm 3. Grade 3 events included 1 instance each of adrenal insufficiency, increased amylase, nausea, liver function test abnormalities, CK increase, and rash. The overall number of adverse events was similar between study arms. Adverse events that were likely immune-related, including grade 1 events, were more prevalent in patients treated in Arm 2 (21/30, 70%) compared with Arm 1 (12/30, 40% online supplemental table 1). Specifically evaluating irAE >grade 1, 18/60 (30%) patients overall experienced an irAE, 7/30 (23%) in Arm A, and 11/30 (37%) in Arm B. The most common adverse events were fatigue (19/60, 32%), rash (12/60, 20%), and thyroid dysfunction (8/60, 13%), but most of these were grade 1. Of note, three patients in Arm 2 experienced an increase in CK, one of whom also had increases in ALT and AST. CK elevation was not associated with symptoms of myositis, and none of these patients required corticosteroid therapy. Three other patients in Arm 2 experienced increases in ALT and/or AST. In contrast, one patient in Arm 1 experienced grade 1 AST elevation, and no patients in that arm experienced creatine kinase elevation. Overall, six patients required corticosteroid therapy for documented or presumed irAE (pneumonitis (n=3), nausea, hepatitis, and arthralgias), and five patients (three in Arm A and two in Arm B) discontinued therapy due to adverse effects. With the exception of one individual who developed adrenal insufficiency, all other grade 3 and 4 events did resolve.

sec.title: Immunological response
sec.p: Blood was collected from patients treated at one of the clinical trial sites (n=27) for immune analyses. Patients were evaluated for IFNγ-secreting T cell immune responses to the vaccine target antigens (PAP and AR), PSA as a prostate-specific but negative control, and tetanus as a positive control. As shown in figure 2, persistent post-treatment immune responses were infrequent. Immune responses (significant responses detected at least twice in the post-treatment period) to PAP were detected in 1/14 (7%) patients treated in Arm A, and 2/13 (15%) patients treated in Arm B. As expected, persistent immune responses to AR were only detected in patients treated in Arm B (2/13, 15%). No persistent immune responses were detected to PSA, and immune responses to tetanus were detected in only 2/27 (7%) patients. Changes in immune response from baseline for each antigen are shown in online supplemental figure 1. While a couple of patients appeared to have decreased immune response to individual proteins over time, this was largely due to pre-existing high pretreatment response to these proteins (online supplemental figure 2).

caption.title: Immunological response—IFNγ ELISPOT. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells were collected from a subset of subjects treated at one center (n=14, Arm A; n=13, Arm B) at baseline, 6 weeks, 12 weeks, 24 weeks, 36 weeks, and 48 weeks and evaluated for antigen-specific IFNγ secretion by ELISPOT. Shown is a heat map indicating presence of an antigen-specific immune response (red) that was statistically significant compared with media only, threefold greater in magnitude than baseline, and with a frequency of at least 1:100 000 cells. Black indicates no immune response, and uncolored indicates no evaluation (patient off trial or sample not available). AR, androgen receptor; PAP, prostatic acid phosphatase; PSA, prostate-specific antigen.

sec.p: We hypothesized that changes in serum levels of cytokines associated with T cell activation or T cell recruitment might be detectable in sera samples, as previously observed in previous trials using vaccine and PD-1 blockade.18 21 Consequently, serum samples obtained pretreatment and at week 6 were evaluated for changes in 35 cytokines and chemokines by Luminex analysis or ELISA for the same 27 patients. Significant changes were observed for G-CSF (figure 3A), CCL11 (figure 3B), HGF (figure 3C), and IL-1Rα (figure 3D), with similar changes in either treatment arm. Decreases in IL-4 were observed in patients treated in Arm A, but not Arm B. Of note, there were no significant changes in CXCL9, CXCL10, or IFNγ that had been observed in previous trials using vaccine and PD-1 blockade.18 21

caption.title: Treatment elicited changes in some serum cytokines and chemokines. Sera samples were obtained from the same subset of patients as shown in figure 2 prior to treatment and at week 6 of treatment. These were evaluated for 35 cytokines and chemokines by multiplex Luminex assay. Shown are the changes in concentration from baseline for each patient, grouped by study arm (Arm A=blue, Arm B=red), for those cytokines with significant change over time (by paired t test). (A) granulocyte-colony stimulating factor (G-CSF), (B) C-C motif chemokine ligand 11 (CCL11), (C) hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), (D) IL-1Rα, and (E) IL-4. Given that these were exploratory studies, no corrections were made for multiple comparisons.

sec.title: Clinical effects
sec.p: PSA values were obtained every 3 weeks. Shown in figure 4A is the “best” PSA change (greatest decrease or least increase) compared with D1 of treatment. 19/60 patients (32%) had any PSA decline, 8/30 (27%) in Arm A and 11/30 (37%) in Arm B. 12/60 (20%) had a PSA decline of >50%, 20% in each arm. As shown in figures 4B, 20 patients had measurable disease, of whom 13 had a decrease in tumor volume. Six (30%) had a confirmed partial response. One patient in Arm B without measurable disease had a PSA that declined to undetectable levels. 53% of patients (32/60, 15/30 Arm A and 17/30 Arm B) came off trial prior to 6 months. Overall, 28% (17/60) remained on trial without progression beyond 6 months (6-month disease control rate), 30% (9/30) in Arm A and 27% (8/30) in Arm B. The 6-month PFS rate was 51% in Arm A and 45% in Arm B (p=0.92, figure 4C). Median overall survival was 33.6 months (29.9 months (2.5 years) Arm A and 44.7 months (3.7 years) Arm B, p=0.16, figure 4D). Of note, of patients who had received prior ARPI treatment (48/60, 80%), the median overall survival was 30.6 months, and for those who had received prior taxane chemotherapy and ARPI (14/60, 23%), the median overall survival was 25.3 months. There was little difference in overall survival among patients who had received few versus extensive prior treatments for mCRPC (online supplemental figure 3).

caption.title: Clinical effects. (A) Serum PSA values were collected from all individuals prior to treatment and over the course of treatment. Shown is the best percentage change in serum PSA from day 1. Red lines show individual patients treated in Arm A, and blue lines show individual patients treated in Arm B. (B) The best percentage change in tumor volume for the 20 individuals who had measurable disease. Kaplan-Meier curves for time to progression (C) and overall survival (D) by treatment arm. (E) Serum PSA values for an individual patient who completed 2 years of treatment. Time points at which he received pembrolizumab±vaccine cycles are shown. (F) Serum PSA values for an individual patient who received subsequent booster cycles of vaccine without pembrolizumab. PSA, prostate-specific antigen.

sec.p: At 6 months, vaccinations were stopped and patients continued to be treated with pembrolizumab for up to 2 years. Two patients, one in each arm, completed 2 years of treatment. The PSA curve for one such patient is shown in figure 4E. Eight patients had evidence of PSA progression (25% rise in PSA from the time of stopping vaccination), without radiographic progression, and went on to receive additional cycles of vaccine. Three of these individuals had evidence of subsequent PSA decline (online supplemental figure 4). In one particular case (shown in figure 4F), a patient developed grade 2 liver function test abnormalities at cycle 8, and biopsy confirmed mild hepatitis. Pembrolizumab was discontinued, but he remained on study and received vaccine booster immunizations at the times of subsequent PSA progression. As shown, he experienced a decline in PSA following the first set of four booster immunizations, but not the second.

There was no association between time to progression or overall survival and the development of antigen-specific immune response (online supplemental figure 5). Patients who developed a PSA50 response (figure 5A), however, or who remained on treatment beyond 6 months without progression (figure 5B), tended to have a longer overall survival, although these differences were not statistically significant. Similarly, those who developed irAE of any grade tended to have a longer overall survival, although this was not statistically significant. Testing for MSI was not required for eligibility, but was available for 34/60 (57%) patients. Of these individuals, 1/34 (3%) had MSI-H tumors. That individual did not experience a PSA decline, PR, and had radiographic progression at 6 months. Among patients who experienced a PR, 4/6 were confirmed to have microsatellite stable (MSS) disease, and among patients with a PSA decline >50%, 7/12 were confirmed to have MSS disease. A summary of prior treatments, MSI status, immune response, and clinical outcomes for each patient is shown in online supplemental table 2.

caption.title: Associations with overall survival. Overall survival was assessed with respect to PSA decline by greater than 50% (A), whether patients remained on treatment without progression at 6 months (B), or by whether they experienced an irAE of any grade (C) (as in online supplemental table 1). (B) Conducted as a landmark analysis at 6 months, excluding the five patients who died or experienced progression prior to 6 months. Statistical comparisons are made using a log-rank test, with p<0.05 considered statistically significant. irAE, immune-related adverse event; PSA, prostate-specific antigen.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: We report here the results of a randomized phase 2 trial evaluating one versus two DNA vaccines, in combination with PD-1 blockade, as treatment for mCRPC. The primary objective was to determine if using vaccines targeting more than one tumor-associated antigen would lead to improved clinical efficacy as measured by time to progression. This was not observed. Notwithstanding, for both treatment arms, there was evidence of clinical activity as demonstrated by PSA declines, and notably PSA declines that were not related to PD-1 blockade alone, objective changes in tumor volumes, and survival greater than expected when compared with similar studies conducted with PD-1 blockade alone or with other approved agents. While adverse effects were similar between the treatment arms, and no new safety concerns were identified, these were slightly more frequent in patients receiving two vaccines. Taken together, these findings suggest that future studies using DNA vaccines and PD-1 blockade as treatment for prostate cancer may not require two antigens, or at least not only the two antigens (PAP and AR) evaluated here.

The primary endpoint, 6-month PFS rate, was not statistically different between the study arms. The median time to progression was 24 weeks for both Arm A and Arm B. Similarly, while the overall survival tended to be longer for patients treated in Arm B (44.7 months vs 29.9 months), this was not statistically significant (p=0.16). There was a slight imbalance in the number of patients with visceral metastases, with more patients in Arm B having visceral metastases, suggesting that this might have impacted the survival analysis. However, even excluding from analysis those patients with visceral metastases, there was not a significant difference in PFS (48.1 weeks vs 24.4 weeks, p=0.54, log-rank test) or overall survival (45.5 months vs 29.9 months, p=0.12) between the study arms (data not shown). While these findings suggest there is not an advantage in using two vaccines relative to one vaccine, they still compare favorably to what has been reported in contemporary clinical trials with other agents used in combination with pembrolizumab. For example, in a phase 3 trial of enzalutamide with or without pembrolizumab for patients who had not received chemotherapy for mCRPC, the median overall survival was 24.7 or 27.3 months.26 Similarly, in a recently reported phase 3 trial of docetaxel with or without pembrolizumab for patients with mCRPC who had received one ARPI, the median overall survival was 19.6 or 19.0 months.27 While the current trial enrolled patients with mCRPC irrespective of prior therapies, and hence these are not directly comparable, the overall survival observed was over 30 months, even in patients with advanced disease who had received multiple prior therapies. Our findings are consistent with a previous trial using pTVG-HP and pembrolizumab, evaluating different sequences and schedules of administration in 66 patients with mCRPC, in which we observed 32% of patients who remained on treatment without progression over 6 months, and an overall median survival of 22.9 months.18

Immune responses to the vaccine target antigens in peripheral blood samples were only detected in a few patients in the current trial. As a result, there was no detectable association between immune response and favorable clinical outcomes. These rates were below what we have previously observed in trials using pTVG-HP or pTVG-AR.18 24 In addition, we had previously observed changes in serum cytokines and chemokines associated with T-cell activation and recruitment, including IFNγ, IL-12, IL-2, IFNα, CXCL9, and CXCL10.18 Changes in these were not observed in the current trial at a similar 6-week time point. We speculate that these differences may be related to the vaccine schedule, as we had previously observed decreases in immune response rates when vaccines were given every 3 weeks compared with every 2 weeks.18 24 In that trial, we had also observed longer time to progression in patients receiving vaccine every 2 weeks and pembrolizumab every 4 weeks; however, in the current trial, we were obligated to design a schedule accommodating the approved schedule of pembrolizumab used every 3 weeks. It is conceivable that the current schedule, in which patients received vaccines weekly × 2, repeated every 3 weeks, designed to facilitate use with standard every-3-week dosing of pembrolizumab, resulted in vaccinations being delivered at too-frequent intervals. Notably, most of the immune responses detected were within the early post-treatment time points, suggesting the possibility that immune responses were lost over time. There is little information about optimal vaccination schedules for cancer vaccines in humans. A study by Da Silva et al, however, using a murine tumor model found that administration of an anti-tumor vaccine at weekly intervals led to potent effector cells and anti-tumor efficacy, but was less effective in eliciting long-term protective immunity than schedules with a longer interval between booster immunizations.28 Ultimately, immune changes occurring in the tumor are most critical to studying the mechanisms of action and resistance, and hence studies evaluating immune changes in tumor tissues will be prioritized in future studies. In any case, the vaccinations used appear to be key components of this combination therapy, particularly because PSA declines were observed in some patients treated with subsequent booster immunizations. In previous trials using the pTVG-HP vaccine alone, while changes in PSA rate of rise were observed, PSA declines were not.20 Hence, the PSA declines observed are consistent with a combination effect, PD-1 blockade with vaccination, and not either alone, as we have observed in animal models.16 Collectively, these findings suggest that tumor-specific T-cell activation, whether by anti-tumor vaccination or potentially other T-cell activating therapies, needs to accompany PD-1 blockade for PD-1 blockade therapy to be effective in the treatment of prostate cancer.

While there were no unexpected toxicities observed, and no new safety concerns, we did see a slightly higher frequency of grade 1–2 adverse events in patients in Arm B, and greater numbers of irAE in patients treated in Arm B. Specifically, 18/60 (30%) had irAE >Grade 1, 7/30 (23%) in Arm A, and 11/30 (37%) in Arm B. Curiously, this was at a lower rate than what we had previously observed in a similar population of patients treated with pTVG-HP and pembrolizumab, in which 28/66 (42%) patients experienced irAE>grade 1.18 In that trial, the development of irAE was associated with prolonged overall survival.18 While the development of irAE was loosely associated with increased survival in the current trial, this was not statistically significant. We do not know why rates of irAE would be different, although we suspect this was also related to the change in vaccine schedule. We did previously observe that patients with irAE tended to have immune-related changes in the tumor similar to patients with tumor response (PSA decline), suggesting that irAE may be associated with favorable anti-tumor immunity.29 Consistent with this, most patients who developed a PSA50 response and/or radiologic response also experienced an irAE in the current trial (online supplemental table 2). Among the irAE observed, patients in Arm B experienced more increases in CK and/or transaminases. While these were not statistically different between the study arms, they do raise the possibility that these individuals receiving the AR-targeted vaccine could have had increased autoimmune toxicity to other tissues (eg, liver and/or muscle) that also express AR.

Major limitations of the current trial were the relatively small sample size and the absence of a pure control group. The trial was powered to detect a large difference in time to progression, and in fact, patients treated in Arm A had a 6-month PFS rate of 51%, greater than the hypothesized rate of 20%–25%. This rate of 20%–25% had been chosen based on the results from contemporary randomized trials using ARPI as one of the treatment arms.30 31 Thus, it is conceivable that a larger trial might have demonstrated a slight increase in time to progression. In addition, when this trial was designed, pembrolizumab had not yet been approved for MSI-H tumors, and hence MSI testing was not required as an entry criterion. Unfortunately, it was not possible to obtain this information for all individuals. While it is conceivable that some of the clinical responses observed were due to expected pembrolizumab treatment of occult MSI-H tumors, this seems unlikely given that only 1/34 tumors for which testing was available was found to be MSI-H. Moreover, most of the clinical responses (major PSA declines and objective responses) were observed in patients who did not have MSI-H tumors, and the one patient with documented MSI-H disease did not experience a clinical response. While not powered to detect differences in survival, we did observe a slight, yet not statistically significant, increase in overall survival in patients treated in Arm B. Notwithstanding, given that there were no large or statistically significant differences in clinical endpoints, the fact that clinical endpoints observed were still better than anticipated given other contemporary trials in this population, and the possibility that there might have been slightly greater toxicity with two vaccines. Future trials will proceed using pTVG-HP alone with PD-1 blockade and using a vaccine schedule fixed at 2-week intervals as previously evaluated.18 We are currently planning a randomized phase 2 trial using pTVG-HP and PD-1 blockade versus standard of care in patients with advanced mCRPC who have received prior taxane and ARPI treatment.
